# `•float` — Float width

`16 •float Y`, `32 •float Y` and `64 •float Y` give the numbers of `Y` as floats of that many bits. Each number rounds to the nearest float of the width. A complex number's parts round to the width, or to 32 bits for 16. Arrays nested in `Y` convert too. Under [`∂`](../glyphs/partial.qmd), a tangent converts with its primal. A gradient keeps its argument's width, whatever width the function computes at. [Float widths](../numbers.qmd#float-widths) gives the rules that floats of each width follow.

```bpl
v←32 •float 0.1 0.2 0.3
(•storage v).kind              ⍝ "float32"
(•storage 64 •float v).kind    ⍝ "float64"
```

`•float Y` gives the width of `Y`'s floats, as a number that `•float`'s left argument takes. It's the widest float width among the numbers in `Y`, nested arrays included. When they're all exact, it's the default width, which the `float` setting of [`•prefs`](prefs.qmd) chooses. Code that writes its constants as `(•float x)•float c` runs at whatever width its data `x` has:

```bpl
x←16 •float 1 2 3
•float x                                ⍝ 16ₓ
(•storage x×(•float x)•float 0.5).kind   ⍝ "float16"
```

Errors: `DOMAIN` for a width other than 16, 32 or 64, and for characters and functions.
